metaTitle: Good Light for Selfies: A Two-Minute Guide Before You Upload
metaDescription: Good light for selfies takes two minutes: face a window in daylight, phone at eye level, check both cheeks. Why ceiling lights, lamps and flash ruin headshots.
excerpt: Face a window in daylight, hold the phone at eye level, and your selfies are lit well enough for an AI headshot. Here is why overhead lights, evening lamps and flash all fail, a quick self-test for even light, and a two-minute checklist to run before you upload.
quickAnswer: Good light for selfies means daylight from a window in front of you, phone at eye level, with both cheeks lit evenly and both eyes clearly visible. Skip ceiling lights, evening lamps and flash. Light matters more for AI headshots than for a normal selfie because the model learns the face it is shown, so a set of 10 to 12 window-lit photos gives it the true version of you.
content:
Face a window in daylight, hold your phone at eye level, and you are done. That single change fixes more selfies than any app, filter or camera setting. Everything else in this guide is a way to check you actually did it.

What is good light for selfies before you upload?

Good light is soft daylight coming from in front of you, at roughly the height of your face. A window you are facing does this for free: it lights both cheeks, fills in the eye sockets and shows the true colour of your skin. Ceiling lights, bedside lamps and phone flash all light you from the wrong direction or in the wrong colour, and each one leaves a mark the camera cannot undo.

At a glanceWhat to do
Light sourceA window in daylight, sun not shining directly on you
Where the window sitsIn front of you, not behind you and not only to one side
Phone heightEye level, arm's length or propped on a shelf
Time of dayDaytime; an overcast afternoon is ideal
Photos to take5 to 15 for Picturesk, 10 to 12 is the sweet spot
Time neededAbout two minutes once you are at the window

Why should the window be in front of you?

Because the camera exposes for the brightest thing it sees. Put the window behind you and the brightest thing is the sky, so your face turns into a dark, grainy shape with a glowing outline. Put the window to one side only and you get one bright cheek, one shadowed cheek and a nose shadow across your face.

Face the window and the light lands on both cheeks at once. Your eyes pick up a small bright reflection, which is what makes a face look awake. Stand close enough that the window fills your view, and step back if the sun is hitting you directly and making you squint.

Why do ceiling lights, lamps and flash fail?

Overhead ceiling light comes from above your head, so your brow shades your eyes, your nose casts a shadow onto your lip and your cheeks go hollow. It is the light that makes everyone look tired in a lift. Even a bright room can do this if the only source is on the ceiling.

The evening lamp has two problems. It is orange, so your skin takes on a cast the camera struggles to correct, and it is dim, so the phone raises its sensitivity and fills the picture with speckled noise. Flash does the opposite and blasts you from the front at close range, flattening every contour and leaving harsh black shadows behind your head.

How do you check the light is even?

Open the camera, look at yourself, and run this test. Can you see both eyes clearly, with colour in them and no dark sockets? Are both cheeks the same brightness, with no hard line down the middle of your nose?

If either answer is no, turn slightly until it is yes. A small quarter turn toward the window usually fixes a one-sided face. If your eyes are still shadowed, lift your chin a touch or move closer to the glass.

Why does light matter more for AI headshots than a normal selfie?

A normal selfie is one photo that one person glances at. An AI headshot generator is different: we train a model on your face from the photos you give it, and the model learns the face it is shown. Feed it dim, orange, shadowed selfies and it learns a dim, orange, shadowed version of you, then reproduces it in a suit.

Research backs up how much light alone can shift what a face seems to say. A 2014 PNAS study found that first impressions vary substantially across different photos of the same person, with lighting, pose and expression moving the judgement. An earlier Cognition paper showed that photos of one unfamiliar face can vary so much that people sort them as different people.

That is why input quality is the biggest lever on whether the results look like you. Picturesk checks every photo before payment for one clear face and uncovered eyes, but it cannot add light that was never there. Consistent window light across all 10 to 12 photos gives the model one true face to learn, and that is what the 3-day look-like-you guarantee rests on.

The two-minute checklist

  1. Go to the biggest window in the house during daylight and turn off the room lights.
  2. Face the window squarely, about an arm's length from the glass.
  3. Raise the phone to eye level, or prop it on a shelf at that height.
  4. Check both eyes are bright and both cheeks match, then turn slightly if they do not.
  5. Take 10 to 12 photos, moving your head a little between each so the angles vary.
  6. Flick through them and delete any where you squinted or the light shifted.

That is the whole job. With those photos on your phone you can start a set with the Picturesk AI headshot generator and have the finished headshots in your inbox in about an hour.

Sources

  • Modeling first impressions from highly variable facial images, PNAS
  • Variability in photos of the same face, Cognition (ScienceDirect)

faqs.question: Is window light really enough for AI headshot selfies?
faqs.answer: Yes. Soft daylight from a window you are facing is the best light most people have access to, and it beats any lamp or ring light in a normal home. It lights both cheeks evenly, keeps colour true and shows your eyes clearly, which is exactly what the model needs to learn your face.

faqs.question: Can I take selfies at night with the lights on?
faqs.answer: Better not. Ceiling lights put shadows under your eyes and nose, and lamps give an orange cast plus noise because the phone has to boost its sensitivity. If you cannot wait for daylight, sit facing the brightest white light you have, at face height, and never rely on flash.

faqs.question: What if the sun is shining straight through the window?
faqs.answer: Step back or move to a window without direct sun. Harsh sunlight makes you squint and creates hard shadows, which is the same problem as flash in reverse. A north-facing window, an overcast day or a thin curtain all soften it to the even light you want.

faqs.question: Should all my selfies have the same light?
faqs.answer: Yes, keep it consistent. Picturesk accepts 5 to 15 photos and 10 to 12 is the sweet spot, but they should all be taken in the same window light within a few minutes. Mixing a bright daylight shot with an orange evening one gives the model two versions of you to reconcile.
